newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-US Treasury to propose broadening bank power.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-US Treasury to propose broadening bank power.

text.p: The elections left the political landscape virtually unchanged for dealing with banking reform and lawmakers were again expected to tackle lifting Depression-era restrictions, industry groups said Wednesday.
The Treasury Department is required to issue a plan by March 31, 1997 for merging the thrift and bank charters to essentially create one industry.
The Treasury proposal will also address the broader issue of allowing banks to engage in various kinds of financial activities, Treasury Undersecretary John Hawke said.
For decades, efforts have failed to tear down the Glass-Steagall Act, a law erected around the Depression to shield banks from the risks of securities activities.
Attempts on that front fell through during this past Congress, but some recent developments give rise to renewed optimism for success, Hawke and industry groups said.
A key factor is that sectors of the insurance industry which had vehemently opposed granting banks greater access to their business, have softened their stance.

The Independent Insurance Agents of America now say they do not plan to oppose proposals that would allow banks to own insurance companies and vice versa if the insurance activities are regulated at the state level.
Hawke said he believes the concerns of the insurance agents can be addressed and bank powers broadened.

"The primary thing that they are concerned about is preserving state regulation over insurance agency activities, and we don't have any problem with that provided ... that it doesn't discriminate against banks," he said in a telephone interview with Reuters.
While Treasury has not firmed up how far it will propose to go on the question of what entities banks should be allowed to affiliate with, it supported broad affiliation, Hawke said.

The plan that Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato, R-NY, proposed in the past Congressional session has "great appeal," Hawke said. D'Amato had proposed allowing affiliations between bank, insurance, securities and commercial companies.

"Our present thinking is that there ought to be broad latitude for banking organizations to engage in activities that are financially related under some broad standard and to affiliate with a wide range of organizations," Hawke said.
"I don't know how far we will go on the affiliations question," he added.

Any post-election changes in the House and Senate Banking committees were expected to be minor, and Rep. James Leach, R-Iowa, and Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, R-NY, were expected to retain chairmanship of the respective committees.
"Overall there isn't much change in terms of complexion of the key players of the last two years," Ed Yingling, executive vice president of the American Bankers Association, said.
"Given that, I think certainly the whole issue of financial modernization and merging of the charters will be a front-burner issue," he said.
